title: The Samadhi in Lahore
hook: his memorial stands beside Lahore Fort, near a gurdwara

segments.voice: Yesterday, the soldiers' councils, which claimed to speak for the Panth, and your line was the army spoke. Whose voice from lower down did you hear? Today we step out of the noise of the court and into a quiet building of stone. Day nine hundred thirty.

Stand in old Lahore with your back to the great walls of the Fort. In front of you rises a pale building with a gilded dome and small domes around it, and arched windows of carved stone. Next to it is a gurdwara. Nearby, the huge red mosque of a Mughal emperor. Inside the pale building, under a canopy, are urns of ashes. This is where the Maharaja who took Lahore came to rest. Today: the Samadhi in Lahore.
screen: `A PALE BUILDING BY THE FORT.` → `A GURDWARA NEXT DOOR.` → `URNS OF ASHES UNDER A CANOPY.`

segments.voice: First, the word. A samadhi, in the Punjab, is a memorial raised over the place where a person was cremated. It isn't a tomb in the usual sense, since there's no body, only ashes and memory. Ranjit Singh's samadhi was begun after his death by his son, and finished in the years of the troubles you've been hearing about. Second, the neighbor. Right beside it stands Gurdwara Dera Sahib, which marks the place where Sikh tradition says Guru Arjan, the Fifth Guru, was martyred in Lahore. So the Maharaja's memorial stands next to the memory of a Guru who gave his life. The two buildings share one courtyard of memory. Third, the Guru's word. Sikh tradition links Guru Arjan's last days in Lahore with a line from one of his own hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib: what you do seems sweet to me, and Nanak asks only for the treasure of the Name. A king's memorial of gold and stone stands beside the memory of a Guru who asked for nothing but the Name. And inside the samadhi, small memorials keep the queens and serving women who died on his pyre, the sorrow from five days ago, close beside him. Fourth, what a memorial does. It keeps a name in one place, so people can come and stand before it. Sikhs from across the border still visit when they can. The building can't tell you everything about the man. But it gives the memory an address. That's today's line.
screen: `A MEMORIAL OVER ASHES.` · `BESIDE THE GURU'S GURDWARA.` · `WHAT YOU DO SEEMS SWEET.` · `A MEMORY WITH AN ADDRESS.` · then, large: `REMEMBERED IN STONE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes at a memorial. Sit, and let your breath slow. In your mind, walk to a place where someone is remembered: a grave, a plaque, a bench with a name on it, a photo on a shelf. Stand in front of it. Notice the stone, the wood, the light. Notice the name. Let one memory of that person, or of what the place stands for, come up by itself. Stay with it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
samadhi, a memorial raised over the place of cremation; the Maharaja's samadhi in Lahore stands beside the Fort and next to Gurdwara Dera Sahib, the place of Guru Arjan's martyrdom. Today's word.
Your line: remembered in stone. Today, look closely at one memorial you pass, a name on a wall or a bench, and read it all the way through. Day nine hundred thirty.
